text: Speculative execution is basically the CPU guessing the future so it doesn't have to wait. But when the guess is wrong, the rollback isn't nearly as clean as we assumed.
context: Modern CPUs speculatively execute instructions beyond unresolved branches, discarding results if the prediction is wrong—branch misprediction costs 10–20 cycles. Spectre and Meltdown revealed that speculative execution leaves microarchitectural side-effects (cache state) observable even when its architectural effects are rolled back, breaking the isolation assumed by the entire virtual memory model. Mitigations like retpoline and IBRS carry measurable throughput costs of 5–30% on workloads with indirect branches. The live tension is that the performance of modern systems is inseparable from speculative execution, and the security of modern systems requires constraining it—these are formally incompatible goals at the microarchitectural level.

Spectre and Meltdown revealed that speculative execution leaves microarchitectural side-effects (cache state) observable even when its architectural effects are rolled back, breaking the isolation assumed by the entire virtual memory model. Mitigations like retpoline and IBRS carry measurable throughput costs of 5–30% on workloads with indirect branches. The live tension is that the performance of modern systems is inseparable from speculative execution, and the security of modern systems requires constraining it—these are formally incompatible goals at the microarchitectural level.
